question: What first drew you to creative writing?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific moment or habit that shows writing has been a real practice, not a vague love of reading.

bullets: Name a concrete moment, teacher, book, or habit that started it
Show how it grew from a spark into ongoing practice
Avoid a generic 'I've always loved stories' answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started keeping a notebook in year eight after a teacher read one of my short stories aloud to the class, and something about seeing my own sentences land with an audience hooked me. I kept writing after that, mostly bad fantasy fiction at first, just because I wanted to chase that feeling again. Somewhere around sixteen it stopped being about that first rush and became something I needed to do most days, even when nobody was reading it.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always loved reading' with no specific writing moment
Describing themselves as a reader rather than a writer
Giving an answer that could apply to any humanities subject
followUps: What's changed about your writing since that first moment?

subtopic: Writing as more than a hobby
question: Plenty of people write in their spare time. Why do you want to study it formally rather than just keep doing it on your own?
lookingFor: Understanding of what structured study, workshop culture, and feedback add that solo writing can't.

bullets: Acknowledge what they've gained from writing alone
Identify a specific limit of writing in isolation
Explain what structured feedback or study would add
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Writing alone has taught me a lot, but I've hit a ceiling where I can't always tell what isn't working in my own drafts, I'm too close to them. What I want from a formal course is regular, honest feedback from people whose judgment I trust, and the discipline of deadlines that push me past my comfort genre. I also want to be taught craft properly rather than picking it up in fragments from writing blogs.

commonMistakes: Implying formal study is only about credentials
Dismissing the value of independent writing entirely
Not naming what feedback or structure specifically offers
followUps: What's the most useful piece of feedback you've ever received on your writing?

question: Why do you want to study creative writing at our university specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this program's structure, faculty, or approach, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific feature: workshop model, a faculty member's work, a genre strength
Connect it to their own writing needs or goals
Show they understand how this differs from other programs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read that your program runs small workshops from first year rather than saving them for upper levels, and that matters to me because I've never had regular peer critique before. I also came across a short story collection by one of your faculty members that deals with unreliable narration in a way I've been trying and failing to pull off myself, and I'd love to study under someone thinking about that problem seriously. Compared to programs that are mostly lecture-based until the final year, yours seems built around the actual practice of writing from the start.

commonMistakes: Praising the university's reputation with no course-specific detail
Naming a feature that doesn't actually exist in the program
Giving an answer that would fit any creative writing course
followUps: What would you want to bring to a workshop with your peers?

question: Why creative writing rather than English literature, if you clearly love reading too?
lookingFor: A clear sense that they want to produce work, not only analyze it, while still valuing literary study.

bullets: Show respect for literary study rather than dismissing it
Explain the specific pull toward making rather than analyzing
Note that reading closely still feeds their own writing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I do love literary analysis and I'll keep reading critically no matter what I study, but what I actually want to spend my days doing is making things, not writing about what other people made. Studying a novel's structure is useful to me mainly because I want to steal the technique for my own stories. Creative writing lets me keep both, close reading in service of my own drafts, rather than analysis as the end point.

commonMistakes: Dismissing literary study as less valuable
Being unable to articulate the actual difference between the two
Suggesting they dislike close reading, which undercuts their reading answers elsewhere
followUps: How do you think reading critically has changed the way you write?

question: Who is a writer who has influenced you, and how does that show up in your own work?
lookingFor: A specific, well-understood influence with a concrete link to their own writing choices.

bullets: Name a specific writer or book, not a vague genre
Explain what technique or quality they admire
Show a real link to a choice in their own writing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: George Saunders is the writer I keep going back to, especially for the way he uses humor right next to real sadness without either one undercutting the other. I noticed that after reading Tenth of December I started letting my own short stories be funnier, where before I thought seriousness meant being solemn all the time. My last story has a joke in the middle of a hospital waiting room scene that I don't think I'd have risked before I read him.

commonMistakes: Naming a favorite author with no specific technique mentioned
Claiming influence that doesn't show anywhere in their own work
Picking someone they clearly haven't read closely
followUps: What's a technique of theirs you haven't managed to pull off yet?

question: What have you read recently outside of your school or college reading list?
lookingFor: Evidence of independent, active reading, ideally across genres, with genuine opinions formed.

bullets: Name something specific and recent, not a set-text
Show they read outside their default comfort genre
Offer an actual opinion or reaction, not just a summary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I just finished Ocean Vuong's On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous, which I picked up because I'd only read his poetry before and wanted to see how that lyricism survives in a novel. It mostly does, though I found the fragmented structure harder to stay oriented in than his poems, where the white space does more work. I've also been working through a short story collection by Kevin Barry to push myself toward reading more contemporary Irish writers, since most of what I read growing up was American.

commonMistakes: Naming only assigned school texts
Giving a plot summary instead of a reaction
Naming a book they clearly haven't actually read
followUps: What's something you read that you actively disliked, and why?

question: Talk me through the piece you submitted. What were you trying to do with it, and where do you think it falls short?
lookingFor: Clear intention behind the piece and honest, specific self-critique, not defensive praise of their own work.

bullets: State the piece's central aim or problem it's chasing
Name one specific choice they're proud of
Name a genuine weakness or unresolved problem, specifically
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The piece I submitted is a short story told from the point of view of a kid who doesn't fully understand that his parents are separating, and I was trying to get tension from the gap between what he notices and what the reader can infer. I'm proud of the ending, where he counts the boxes in the hallway without naming what they mean, that restraint took a lot of drafts to earn. Where it still falls short is the middle section, I think I explain his confusion a bit too directly in one paragraph and it breaks the trust I built with the reader.

commonMistakes: Describing the plot instead of the intention behind it
Refusing to name any real weakness in their own work
Being so self-critical it reads as false modesty
followUps: If you had another draft to write, what's the first thing you'd change?

question: Do you have a genre or form you're drawn to, fiction, poetry, nonfiction, script, and why that one?
lookingFor: A genuine, examined preference, with openness to exploring other forms rather than rigid narrowness.

bullets: Name a genre or form with a real reason, not just familiarity
Explain what that form lets them do that others don't
Show openness to trying other forms during the course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm most drawn to short fiction because I like the discipline of having to earn every sentence, there's no room to coast the way a novel sometimes lets you. I did try poetry for a while and I still write it occasionally, but I found I think in scenes and dialogue more naturally than in image and line. That said, I know short stories can get baggy if I only ever write in one form, so I'm looking forward to being pushed into scriptwriting, which I've never seriously attempted.

commonMistakes: Naming a genre only because it's what they've always done, with no reasoning
Dismissing other genres as lesser
Claiming to be equally strong in everything with no real preference
followUps: What's a form you've never tried but would like to?

question: Creative writing courses involve having your work critiqued by peers, sometimes harshly. How do you handle that?
lookingFor: Evidence they can separate their work from their ego and use critical feedback productively, from real experience.

bullets: Give a real example of receiving tough feedback
Show they can distinguish useful critique from unhelpful comments
Explain what they actually did with the feedback afterward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In a summer workshop, someone told me my dialogue all sounded like me rather than like distinct characters, which stung because I'd thought the dialogue was the strongest part of the piece. I sat with it for a day rather than reacting straight away, and once the sting wore off I could see they were right, my characters did all share the same rhythm of speech. I went back and gave each character a distinct verbal habit, and it's something I now check for in every draft. I've learned that the feedback that stings the most is often the most useful.

commonMistakes: Claiming they've never received harsh feedback
Describing getting defensive or dismissing the critique
Saying they'd simply accept all feedback without any judgment
followUps: Has anyone ever given you feedback you disagreed with? What did you do?

question: Do you have a writing routine, and what does it actually look like?
lookingFor: A believable, specific account of how they actually write, not an idealized routine they don't keep.

bullets: Describe something specific and real, including the messy parts
Show consistency or a real attempt at discipline
Avoid describing an unrealistically perfect routine
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I write most mornings before school for about thirty minutes, mostly because it's the only time nobody needs anything from me. It's not glamorous, half the time it's just me staring at a sentence I wrote the day before trying to work out why it's wrong. I don't always hit a word count, but I've learned that showing up on the bad days matters more than the good ones, since the good ones tend to take care of themselves.

commonMistakes: Describing an unrealistically disciplined routine that sounds rehearsed
Claiming to only write when inspired
Giving no specific detail about when or how they actually write
followUps: What do you do on the days the routine breaks down?

question: Walk me through how you revise a piece. What's the biggest cut you've ever made?
lookingFor: A real revision process beyond proofreading, including willingness to cut material they liked.

bullets: Describe an actual multi-stage process, not just correcting typos
Distinguish revision from line-editing
Give a specific example of cutting something they were attached to
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually leave a draft alone for at least a few days before I reread it, because I can't see structural problems while I'm still inside the story. On the second pass I'm only looking at whether scenes earn their place, not fixing sentences yet, that comes much later. The biggest cut I've made was an entire opening page of backstory in a short story, I loved the writing in it, but it was delaying the actual story starting, and the piece got noticeably stronger once I let it go.

commonMistakes: Describing revision as only fixing spelling and grammar
Claiming they never need to cut anything they've written
Giving a vague answer with no concrete example
followUps: How do you know when a piece is actually finished?

question: How do you decide what point of view to write a story in?
lookingFor: Understanding that POV is a deliberate craft choice tied to what the story needs to reveal or withhold.

bullets: Explain what different POVs allow or restrict
Connect the choice to a specific story's needs
Show it's a considered decision, not a default habit
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about what the story needs the reader to know and not know. First person is great when the story depends on a narrator's blind spots, because you can only show what they'd actually notice or admit. In one story I wrote about a girl lying to her family, I chose first person specifically so the reader could feel her justifying herself in real time, which third person would have made feel more judgmental from the outside. If I need to move between more than one character's inner life, though, I'll usually switch to close third.

commonMistakes: Treating POV as a purely stylistic preference with no functional reasoning
Confusing first person with unreliable narration as if they're the same thing
Being unable to explain why a specific POV suited a specific story
followUps: Have you ever changed a story's point of view partway through drafting? What happened?

question: What does the advice 'show, don't tell' actually mean to you, and when might telling be the right choice?
lookingFor: A working understanding of the technique plus enough nuance to know it isn't an absolute rule.

bullets: Explain the core idea with a concrete example
Note that telling is sometimes the better craft choice
Avoid treating it as an absolute rule
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: To me it means trusting specific, sensory detail to let the reader feel an emotion rather than naming the emotion directly, so instead of writing that a character is nervous, I might show her checking her phone for the fourth time in a minute. But I don't think telling is always wrong, sometimes a story needs to move quickly through time, and a line like 'the next two years passed quietly' does that job better than dramatizing every month. I think the real skill is knowing which moments deserve the slower, shown treatment.

commonMistakes: Treating it as an absolute rule that telling is always bad
Giving the definition with no concrete example
Confusing 'showing' with simply adding more description
followUps: Can you think of a moment in a book you've read where telling worked better than showing would have?

question: What do you understand by 'voice' in writing, and how would you describe your own?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of voice as distinct from style or plot, plus honest, specific self-assessment.

bullets: Distinguish voice from plot or subject matter
Describe their own voice with specific, not vague, terms
Show awareness that voice can and should still develop
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Voice is the sense of a particular consciousness behind the sentences, the rhythm, the word choices, the things a writer notices that another writer wouldn't. Readers can often tell who wrote something even from a paragraph out of context, and that's voice more than plot or subject. Mine tends to run toward short, plain sentences with occasional long ones that build to something, and I lean on concrete nouns over adjectives. I know it's still developing though, and I can hear how much closer some of my favorite writers get to a voice that feels fully theirs.

commonMistakes: Confusing voice with genre or subject matter
Describing their voice in generic terms like 'descriptive' with no real specificity
Claiming their voice is already fully formed and unchanging
followUps: Has your voice changed noticeably since you started writing seriously?

question: Can you explain what an unreliable narrator is, and why a writer might choose to use one rather than simply telling the reader the truth?
lookingFor: A precise understanding of the technique, an example, and an articulate sense of what it achieves that reliable narration can't.

bullets: Define the technique clearly with an example from reading
Explain what the gap between narrator and truth achieves
Note the risk of the technique if handled badly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An unreliable narrator is one whose account the reader has reason to doubt, whether they're lying, mistaken, or limited by what they can bear to admit to themselves. Nabokov's Humbert Humbert in Lolita is the classic case, he's eloquent and persuasive, but the horror of the story comes from the reader having to read past his justifications to see what's actually happening. I think writers use it because it makes the reader an active participant, working out the truth alongside or against the narrator, which creates a kind of tension that an omniscient, trustworthy narrator can't. The risk is that if the gap is too obscure, readers just feel confused rather than complicit.

commonMistakes: Confusing unreliable narration with simply first person narration
Giving a definition with no real example from actual reading
Not explaining what effect the technique creates for the reader
followUps: Have you attempted an unreliable narrator in your own writing? How did it go?

question: Some people draw a sharp line between literary fiction and genre fiction. What do you think of that distinction?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, non-snobbish view that recognizes the distinction is porous and often overstated.

bullets: Acknowledge the traditional distinction people draw
Push back on it or complicate it with an example
Avoid sounding dismissive of genre fiction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: People usually mean that literary fiction prioritizes language and interiority while genre fiction prioritizes plot and convention, but I think that line gets thinner every year I read. Ursula Le Guin wrote science fiction that's as attentive to sentence and idea as anything called literary, and plenty of literary fiction has weak, meandering plots that could learn something from genre discipline. I don't think the label tells you much about quality, it tells you more about which shelf a bookstore puts it on.

commonMistakes: Dismissing genre fiction as automatically less serious
Accepting the distinction uncritically with no examples
Being unable to name any writer who blurs the line
followUps: Is there a genre convention you'd like to borrow for your own literary work?

question: In poetry, what's a line break actually doing, and how do you decide where to break a line?
lookingFor: A working sense of line breaks as meaning-making rather than arbitrary, with an example.

bullets: Explain that line breaks control pacing, emphasis, or ambiguity
Give a concrete example of a break creating a double meaning or pause
Show awareness of the difference between free verse and formal choices
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A line break controls how a reader breathes and where their attention lands, it can create a pause, a surprise, or even a brief double meaning before the next line resolves it. I remember writing a line that ended on the word 'nothing', and then the next line completed the sentence to mean something quite different, that little swerve wouldn't exist in prose. In free verse I break mostly by ear and by where I want emphasis to fall, but I've also worked in form, like a sonnet, where the meter does some of that deciding for you and the challenge is different.

commonMistakes: Treating line breaks as arbitrary or purely about where the page runs out of room
Giving a definition with no concrete example of a break doing work
Dismissing formal poetry as irrelevant to their own free verse practice
followUps: Have you written in a fixed form, like a sonnet or villanelle? What did you learn from the constraint?

question: Would you describe your writing as more plot-driven or character-driven, and what's the difference to you?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of the distinction and honest self-placement, without dismissing the other mode.

bullets: Define the distinction in their own words
Place their own work honestly on that spectrum
Show the two aren't fully separable in good fiction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: To me plot-driven writing is propelled mainly by external events, what happens next, while character-driven writing is propelled by a character's internal shifts, what they realize or change their mind about. My own stories lean character-driven, I usually start with a person's contradiction and build outward from there, plot tends to arrive almost as a byproduct. That said, I don't think the two are ever fully separate, even the most internal story needs something to actually happen, or nothing changes.

commonMistakes: Claiming pure plot or pure character with no acknowledgment of overlap
Being unable to place their own work honestly on the spectrum
Confusing plot with simply 'things happening' without structure
followUps: Can you think of a story where the plot exists mainly to force a character to change?

question: What makes dialogue feel realistic on the page, and how do you approach writing it?
lookingFor: Understanding that realistic dialogue is a crafted illusion, not a literal transcript, with a concrete technique named.

bullets: Note that real speech transcribed verbatim usually reads badly
Name a specific technique: subtext, interruption, distinct rhythm per character
Give a real example from their own writing or reading
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Realistic dialogue isn't actually realistic in the literal sense, if you transcribe how people really talk it's full of filler and repetition that reads terribly on the page. What makes it feel alive instead is subtext, characters rarely say exactly what they mean, so I try to write toward what's underneath the line rather than the line itself. I also try to give each character a distinct rhythm, one who interrupts, one who trails off, so you could tell them apart even without the tags. In my own writing I struggled with this for a long time, everyone sounded like me until I started reading dialogue out loud to check.

commonMistakes: Believing realistic dialogue means transcribing real speech literally
Giving no concrete technique, just saying dialogue should 'sound natural'
Not distinguishing between characters' speech patterns
followUps: Read us a line of dialogue you're proud of, and tell us why it works.

question: Where do your ideas for stories or poems usually come from?
lookingFor: A believable, specific source of material, showing they observe and collect from real life rather than waiting for inspiration.

bullets: Name a specific, real source: overheard conversation, image, question
Show that ideas are actively noticed and collected, not just waiting to strike
Give one concrete example that became an actual piece
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Most of my ideas start small, an overheard line, an odd detail, rather than a whole plot arriving at once. I keep a notes app full of fragments, and a story I'm proud of started from overhearing my neighbor apologize to her dog for something that clearly wasn't the dog's fault, I couldn't stop thinking about who she was really apologizing to. I've learned that waiting around for a big idea rarely works for me, it's more that I collect small strange things and eventually two of them click together.

commonMistakes: Claiming ideas simply 'come to them' with no active process described
Giving an answer with no concrete example
Describing only borrowing plots from existing books or films
followUps: Do you keep any kind of notebook or record of ideas? What's in it?

question: If you write from personal experience, how do you handle writing about real people in your life, family members, friends, without it becoming a betrayal of them?
lookingFor: Genuine ethical reasoning about using lived material, showing care without being paralyzed into avoiding honest writing.

bullets: Acknowledge the real tension between honesty and loyalty
Describe a concrete practice: changing details, fictionalizing composite characters, or checking in with people
Land on a position rather than avoiding the question
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's something I think about a lot, because the material closest to me is often the material that matters most to write about. My practice is usually to fictionalize enough that the piece isn't a literal transcript of anyone's life, changing details or combining two people into one character, so I'm being honest about an emotional truth without exposing someone's actual private life. For anything closer to memoir, I've started sharing drafts with the people involved before I'd ever publish something, not to ask permission for the truth, but because I think it's fair they're not blindsided. I don't think avoiding the material altogether is the answer, some of the most honest writing comes from exactly the stuff that's hardest to write about.

commonMistakes: Claiming they'd never write anything uncomfortable, avoiding the real question
Having no actual practice or safeguard, just saying 'I'd be careful'
Treating the ethical tension as if it doesn't exist
followUps: Has a piece of your writing ever caused a real conversation or conflict with someone it was based on?

question: What do you do when you're stuck and the writing just isn't coming?
lookingFor: A practical, honest strategy for working through creative stalling, not a claim they never struggle.

bullets: Admit that blocks happen rather than denying it
Describe a specific, practical strategy they actually use
Show they distinguish a genuine block from a piece that needs rethinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It happens to me more than I'd like, usually when I've been trying to force a scene to go somewhere it doesn't actually want to go. When that happens I've learned not to just sit and stare at the same paragraph, I'll switch to writing something completely different for a day, even just journaling, to take the pressure off. Sometimes the block is actually a sign that something earlier in the piece is wrong, so I'll go back and reread from the start rather than pushing forward blindly.

commonMistakes: Claiming they never experience writer's block
Describing only waiting passively for inspiration to return
Not distinguishing a temporary stall from a structural problem in the piece
followUps: Has a block ever taught you something was wrong with the piece itself?

question: How much research do you think fiction needs, and how do you know when you've done enough?
lookingFor: Understanding that research serves the story rather than becoming an end in itself, with a real example.

bullets: Explain research should serve believability, not overload the page
Give a concrete example of research they've done for a piece
Show judgment about when research becomes procrastination
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think fiction needs enough research that the reader trusts the world, but not so much that the story turns into a lecture, most of what you learn should stay invisible under the surface. For a story I wrote about a wildfire, I read accounts from actual firefighters mostly to get small sensory details right, the way ash gets in your throat, rather than the technical firefighting procedure itself. I know I've done enough when I stop learning new things that change how a scene feels, and start learning things that are just interesting but not useful, that's usually my sign to stop and actually write.

commonMistakes: Believing fiction needs no research at all if it's imaginative
Letting research become a way to avoid actually drafting
Overloading a piece with researched detail that isn't load-bearing
followUps: What's the most unusual thing you've had to research for a piece of writing?

question: Why might a writer choose to tell a story out of chronological order, and what are the risks of doing that?
lookingFor: Sophisticated understanding of structure as a deliberate tool, with awareness of the technique's failure modes.

bullets: Explain a specific effect nonlinear structure achieves that linear order can't
Reference a real example from reading
Name the genuine risk of confusing or losing the reader
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A writer might break chronology to control what the reader knows and when, so that a later scene recontextualizes an earlier one rather than just following events in order. In Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, the fragmented timeline mirrors the way the investigation itself uncovers the truth piece by piece, so the structure isn't decoration, it's doing the same work as the plot. The risk is real though, if the reader can't track where they are in time, they stop trusting the story rather than feeling intrigued by it, so I think the technique only earns its place if the confusion is doing something, not just showing off.

commonMistakes: Treating nonlinear structure as inherently more sophisticated with no functional justification
Giving no concrete example from actual reading
Not acknowledging the real risk of losing or confusing the reader
followUps: Have you tried a nonlinear structure in your own writing? What went wrong or right?

question: Very few writers make a full living from creative writing alone. How do you think about that, and what does success look like for you?
lookingFor: Realistic, grounded thinking about the writing life, without either naive fantasy or writing off the ambition entirely.

bullets: Show awareness of the actual economics of a writing career
Describe a realistic plan alongside the ambition, not instead of it
Define personal success in a way that isn't purely about fame or sales
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know the odds of writing being my sole income are slim, and I've looked into what working writers actually do, teaching, editing, journalism, to keep writing alive alongside a day job. That doesn't scare me off it, if anything it makes me want to build practical skills, like editing, that keep me close to the craft even if fiction itself isn't paying every bill. Success to me isn't a bestseller list, it's getting to a point where I'm consistently producing work I'm proud of and getting it in front of readers, even if that's through literary magazines rather than a six-figure book deal.

commonMistakes: Describing an unrealistic plan to support themselves purely through fiction sales
Sounding so pragmatic they seem to have lost the ambition to write at all
Defining success only in terms of fame or bestseller status
followUps: What's a writing-adjacent skill you'd want to build alongside your creative work?
